INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE1
“CR IME” is an unregistered group of people
whose acronym stands for C itizens’ Response to
Increased Muzzle Energy. Its purpose is to provide
an objective logic and framework based on simple
laws of physics to constrain the inherently -
normative question of what level of lethality renders
a firearm “unusually dangerous.” We also wish to aid
this Court in its effort s to practice principled
constitutional decision -making and faithful
originalism. “CRIME” has no parent entity or
issuance of stock. Lee Kranefuss, its founder, started
and ran the global iShares line of ETF ’s for a decade
before taking on business and philanthropic works.
STATEMENT OF THE CASE
A. T
he Measure of Muzzle Energy Per -
Minute (“MEpM”) Defines a Firearm’s
Lethality and Be st Harmonizes the
Cases
 The damage done by a bullet is largely the
result of the amount of energy it has when it leaves
the barrel, which is determined by the weight of the
bullet and its speed. Higher bullet speed makes a
huge difference because energy grows as the square
of speed: doubling speed increases muzzle energy by
a factor of four and increasing it ten -fold produces
100 times more energy. The AR -15 platform rifle can
fire a bullet with a muzzle speed of between 1,140
and 3,479 feet -per-second - which is roughly 2,000

1 No party or party’s counsel authored or financially supported
any of this brief. No person other than a member of the amicus
curiae made such a monetary contribution.

2
miles per hour, or three times the speed of sound.
And, with semiautomatic operation and large,
rapidly-changeable magazines, shooting 60 bullets a
minute is not hard to do.  That means a single
shooter can unleash nearly 60,000 foo t-pounds per
minute of firepower per minute.
 By comparison, a .38 Special handgun delivers
about 300 foot -pounds per minute per shot, and
holds six shots in its cylinder.  If 35 police officers
armed with traditional .38 Specials all empty their
service revolvers in one minute (210 rounds in total),
it would be the equivalent firepower of one person
with an AR-15 rifle. In short, we have come very far
from 1791 in what a gun is and can do, when a
musket was hand-loaded, slow, heavy and long; and,
a capable musketeer might be able to fire four shots
per minute with muzzle energy of 1,129 ft -pounds
per minute -- delivering about 3,900 ft -pounds  per
minute of firepower.2
 MEpM provides an objective measure of how
much lethal energy one person can release in 60
seconds by firearm. The Table compiles the MEpM of
a range of archetypal firearms and cartridges
showing the derivations for each from publicly -
sourced information. Handguns, Semiautomatic
handguns, Bolt-Action rifles, various Semiautomatic
rifles, and AR- 15 platform rifles are arrayed in
ascending rows by MEpM, with columns that show

2 Additionally, musket balls were irregular due to the lack of
precision machining.  Hence, the useful range was 50-100 yards
at best – and an intended target might run out of range before
the musket could be loaded and fired.  All of which is only to
suggest that the Court not require overly specific historical or
regulatory analogues for the outlier-MEpM firearm.

3
the firearm and cartridge, predicate calculations,
and cited source.
Bottom line:  the five weapons with the most
lethality -- by far -- are all archetypal semiautomatic
rifles prohibited under the Connecticut and Cook
County statutes. See Grant Pet. App. 97a -122a
(Conn. Gen. Stat. §§  53-202a(1)(A)(i), (B), (E)(ii));
Viramontes Pet. App. 29a-41a (Code of Ordinances of
Cook County §§ 54 -211(1), (2), (7)(A)(i), (iii), (xix),
(xxxvii)). These firearms have MEpM’s of 12- to-27-
times that of the gold -standard police -issue .38
Special revolver. See  Kranefuss, Lee, “MEpM”
Recent Post, https://lkranefuss.com/mepm/ (last
accessed Oct. 21, 2026), attached as appendix . Our
Table provides an objective measure of how AR -15
rifles’ enhanced bullet velocities and firing capacities
exponentially increase their lethality above and
beyond any other firearm.3
 The Table harmonizes the results in Heller
and Bruen in that all handguns, including
semiautomatics, have relatively -low MEpM’s. We
submit that the Connecticut and Cook County
statutes are over -inclusive in banning such
handguns, and that a more limited ban on AR -15
rifles makes logical sense “without effectively
overruling Heller and severely limiting the Second
Amendment’s protection.” Pet Brief at 4. MEpM also
explains the inherent logic of federal statutes, e.g. ,
18 U.S.C. § 841(d) (flash powder ingredients) and

3 It is worth noting that the AR-15 was a redesign in the
Vietnam War over its World-War-II-era M1 Garand
predecessor, increasing its magazine, reducing recoil, and
shortening the barrel – precisely to increase its lethality, i.e.,
its capacity to kill as many combatants as quickly as possible.
The AK-47 was the Russian equivalent-redesign.

4
cases that proscribe civilian -ownership of artillery
guns, canon, and explosives like dynamite or
detonators, as well as machine guns.
 Ultimately, MEpM warrants this Court’s
attention because it correlates most directly with the
collateral damage cost and public interest. Unlike a
musket ball, a bullet with the MEpM of an AR -15
rifle shatters bones and liquefies organs. See JA8,
JA14-JA16 (correlating muzzle energy with the size
of the radiating wound cavity caused by the
dispersion of kinetic energy), JA41 (referencing
injuries to innocent bystanders shot throug h walls).
The AR- 15 rifle bullet moves with exponentially
greater velocity, since its energy grows as the square
of v. It pierces through the chest, and its supersonic
shockwave pulverizes tissues and blows organs
apart, causing massive internal hemorrhagi ng. It
can also cause collateral damage by penetrating
doors and walls. The kicker is that it can wreak such
havoc in an astonishingly short burst of time.4
 Our Table provides quantitative data with a
clear demarcation line as the best framework for
assessing the States’ regulations. While choosing any
demarcation is, in a sense, subjective, we submit
that it is far more objective than defining “in

4 Connecticut passed its ban, Conn. Gen. Stat. § 53-202, Grant
Pet. App. 97a-122a, in response to the Sandy Hook Elementary
School massacre. There, the shooter, using an AR-15-style
semiautomatic rifle, with 30-round magazines in taped reloads
to reduce reload time, “unleashed 154 5.56-millimeter rounds in
under five minutes[,] [and] killed twenty first-grade students
and six educators.” Grant Pet. App. 5a (emphasis added). While
this Court does not decide cases based on a weapon’s use in a
particular crime, however horrific, it may take notice of the
firing rate, and the harm exacted in minutes, in evaluating a
weapon’s “unusual dangerousness.”

5
common use” “for lawful purposes,” or applying the
historical statute -precursor approach, or the
outlier/state-counting approach to regulation of
implied rights under the Fourteenth Amendment.
Common sense and lived experience tell us that
AR-15 rifles with exponentially -increased MEpM
inflict exponentially-increased carnage.5 This Court’s
Second Amendment jurisprudence should not lose
sight of this, even if Petitioners would cast it aside
as an immaterial “nuance” or an “off -the-table”
policy choice. Pet. Brief at 2, 53. As discussed infra ,
our Table also refutes any notion of linear continuity
in lethality between the “increasingly commonplace”
“repeating firearms” of the 19th Century or the
“semiautomatic technology” of the early 20th
Century, id. at 7, and today’s AR-15 rifles.
 Connecticut, for its part, overlooks the roundsper-minute enhancer, and conflat es semiautomatic
handguns with MEpM’s far below the AR -15 rifle.
See, e.g., Grant Resp. Opp., at 5, 32. The AR -15 rifle
represents a dramatic technological advancement, as
evidenced by its 70% greater MEpM than the next -
closest comparator (aside from the very similar
Russian AK -47 design copied for its lethality from
the AR- 15). See Attachment “A” (comparing .458
Winchester M70 African at 40,259 ft. -pounds per
minute with AR -15 at 68,406). We submit that a
legislature may rely upon this paradigm shift in
MEpM to regulate the AR -15 rifle as an “unusually

5 Petitioners and their amici conflate misuse of handguns
(suicides, accidental discharges, domestic violence, mistaken
identity and bystanders) with use of AR-15 rifles to suggest
that the former are more lethal than the latter. See, e.g., Pet.
Brief at 3. After all, AR-15 rifles were originally designed by
the U.S. Military for battlefield use to cause maximum carnage
in minimum time, and its lethality has stood the test of time.

6
dangerous” firearm, irrespective of whether the
firearm is in “common use.” Cf. Pet. Brief at 46.
 In sum, our Table provides these significant
insights:
• Archetypal semiautomatic handguns, e.g. , the
Beretta 92FS and Glock 22, fire with an
estimated MEpM of 15,408 ft -pounds/minute
and 21,768 ft -pounds/minute, far below those
of comparator AR-15 rifles.

• Archetypal bolt -action rifles, e.g. , the
Remington, Winchester Safari and Winchester
African fire with the h ighest muzzle -energy
per shot, but, by design as big game hunting
and protection weapons do not fire more than
ten rounds per minute with a magazine of
only three, recognizing that only the first one
or two shots can really be effective for that
purpose, and therefore do not produce nearly
as high MEpM (34,120, 34,791, and 40,259
ft./pounds per minute, respectively) as
archetypal semiautomatic rifles that fire at
50% to 110% to 170% more powerful MEpM’s.

• Archetypal semiautomatic rifles such as the
AK-47, A R-15, Browning BAR, M1 Garand,
and Springfield M1A fire at between 60,347
and 108,763 ft. -pounds per minute MEpM’s,
which are orders of magnitude higher than
the other firearms sampled.
 Our Table highlights the bright line between
the Winchester M70 Afri can bolt -action rifle (a so -
called “Elephant Gun”) and the AK -47 because the
latter produces 50% more MEpM, which suggests

7
itself as an objectively -coherent regulatory line that
protects semiautomatic handguns and powerful bolt
action rifles, but excludes semiautomatic rifles.
Neither party nor lower courts draw that same line.
The Court may find our deductive reasoning helpful
should it decide to remand the cases for overbreadth
analysis.
B. The AR -15 Rifle Represents a
Dramatic Technological Change from
Earlier Firearms That Didn’t Warrant
Regulation
Petitioners argue that the AR -15 rifle is the
lineal descendent of Revolutionary Era weaponry
such that side -by-side comparisons with the iconic
Kentucky long -rifle show that the two are “not, by
and large, f undamentally different” in their stocks,
grips, barrel holds or shroud, and forward hand-grip,
none of which make the AR -15 rifle fire faster or
with greater power. Pet. Brief at 5 -8, 8 -11, 17- 22.
But, all of that blinks reality that the AR -15 rifle
inflicts dramatically-greater lethality than any prior
firearms through increased muzzle velocity and rate
of fire (MEpM).
Petitioners trace the AR -15 rifle’s lineage to
the Lewis and Clark expedition with its 22 -round
Girandoni air rifle. Id.  at 7 ( citing Garry, James B.,
Weapons of the Lewis and Clark Expedition , 100–01
(2012). The history lesson is meant to defuse Justice
Barrett’s observation that a lack of regulation during
the Founder’s era should not be mistaken for a
maximalist (“use it or lose it”) e xercise of legislative
power. United States v. Rahimi , 602 U.S. 680, 739-
740 (2024) (Barrett, J., concurring). But, the
Girandoni air rifle shows precisely why Justice
Barrett’s caveat matters.

8
For starters, President Jefferson and
Congress authorized and  funded the journey as an
official U.S. Army expenditure, and Captain
Meriwether Lewis provisioned it from the Harper’s
Ferry arsenal – so this was not an instance of
civilian or militia armament. 6 Moreover, Garry’s
research shows that the Girandoni air ri fle was a
“great curiosity” never used in combat or for hunting,
but rather to impress Native American tribes in
theatrically staged boat -and-river-bank
demonstrations. See Garry, at 97 & n.9. They were
“astonished,” according to Lewis, and “think it is
great medicine which comprehends everything that
is to them incomprehensible.” Id.  at 103 (emphasis
in original).
The Girandoni was not a practical weapon in
any sense. “It took five hundred to a thousand
strokes of a hand pump to fill the air chamber[.]” Id .
at 99. The air reservoir valve was subject to failure
“from something as insignificant as a bit of dirt.”
Garry relates that vulnerability to the weapon
accidentally firing a ball through a woman’s hat 40-
feet away as the expedition set off. Id.  at 94-96, 101.
There is “no other good evidence for Girandoni -style
air rifles having made it to the United States by
[that time].” Id. at 101. Thus, it is a strain to suggest
that this “curiosity” anticipated the AR -15 rifle in

6 Carlos A. Schwantes, The Pacific Northwest: An Interpretive
History 55 (1996); Garry, at 15-16. They also had a swivel gun,
or small cannon, mounted on their keelboat that they fired as a
salute. Garry, at 19, 41, 46. But, no one would suggest that this
brings the cannon or other artillery within the Second
Amendment. See 26 U.S.C. § 5845(f)(2), National Firearms Act,
(classifying these as “destructive devices”).

9
any way, or that any reaso nable inference may be
drawn from the Founders’ lack of regulation.7
Similarly, the Founders’ musket
(Charleville/Model 1785) was inaccurate, slow to
load, required close range, and had a low MEpM of
3,386 ft./lbs. per minute assuming a rate -of-fire of
three rounds per minute. 8 Thus, whatever else may
be said of the ingenuity that led to the development
of the Minié ball, breech-loading, integral cartridges,
bolt-action firing, rifling, smokeless powder, and
repeating mechanisms through the 19th and early
20th centuries, it did not produce a firearm with
more than two -thirds the MEpM of the AK -47, the
least powerful AR -15 rifle. The quantum leap
occurred in 1940 with the development of the
automatic rifle whose design goal was to inflict
maximal battlefield carnage quickly and at short
range. As the lineal descendent of that  dramatic
technological breakthrough in lethality (MEpM), the
AR-15 rifle presents an issue of first principles for
this Court.
In our view, the Second Circuit was right to
discount Petiti oner’s reliance on unregulated
repeating firearms like the Girandoni air rifle from
the founding and reconstruction eras, Grant Pet.
App. 39a -42a, but it did so for the wrong reason.

7 If the Girandoni were plotted out on our Table, it would come
out as follows: weight of bullet 9.5g; muzzle velocity 900 fps;
muzzle-energy 263 ft. pounds, and rpm of 30, for a MEpM of
7,900. That muzzle energy equates to a .38 special, with about
a 50% higher rpm, leading to a MepM also about 50% higher
than a .38 special.

8 The adage “Don’t fire till you see the whites of their eyes,”
often attributed to Col. Putnam at the 1775 Battle of Bunker
Hill, thus reflected on the operational limits of the musket.

10
While “these early multi -shot firearms were neither
reliable nor widely u sed,” their very -low MEpM is
the most cogent explanation why the lack of
regulation presents a poor analogue for the AR -15
rifle.9 That exponential difference in MEpM (7,900
for the Girandoni vs. 60,000-to-108,000 for the AR-15
style rifles) translates dir ectly into rapid carnage in
the hands of a single madman, and that  delta is
what makes the AR -15 rifle a regulatory novelty
with no early-American comparator.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
 Amicus use this brief to present a formula for
assessing t he objective dangerousness of various
firearms and we then connect our answers to the
legal analysis of the question presented. Second
Amendment jurisprudence involves line -drawing
exercises even within an originalist approach. Our

9 The lower court cited evidence consistent with our Table that
the flintlock musket fired with a “muzzle velocity of roughly
1,000 feet per second,” and “[a]s a result they could do much
less harm.” Grant Pet. App. 41a. While that’s the right inquiry,
it lacks completeness. The court noted anecdotally that a semiautomatic rifle can “empty a 30-round magazine in five
seconds,” or in one case, 41 shots in 32 seconds, killing nine and
wounding 17. Id. at 42a. It later accepted the U.S. Army
definition of “rapid semiautomatic fire” as 45-rounds per
minute. Id. at 48a n.27 (citing Dep’t of the U.S. Army, TC 3-
22.9: Rifle and Carbine, § 8-19 (2016).) By contrast, we posit
conservatively 30 rounds per minute for our Table calculation.
The bigger issue: the lower court did not quantify or compare
paradigmatic weapons by rounds-fired-per-minute as an
expression of their MEpM, which is the salient coefficient for
distinguishing AR-15 rifles from all other firearms. See
Kranefuss, Lee, “MEpM” Recent Post,
https://lkranefuss.com/mepm/ (last accessed Oct. 21, 2026),
attached as appendix.

11
measurement tool is an empirical standard that (a)
reconciles a complicated set of cases; and (b) provides
a bright line answer in this case.
 A. T he Muzzle E nergy per M inute
(hereinafter “MEpM”) of any firearm is easily
calculated from basic physics. The formula for
kinetic energy of a moving ob ject is: ( E =
1
2m𝑣𝑣2 per minute x rounds per minute) w here m equals the
mass of the bullet and v equals its velocity upon
leaving the rifle. Thus, doubling the mass (size) of
the bullet doubles the muzzle energy; and doubling
the muzzle velocity makes the muzzle energy four
times as large. Multiplying this number by the
rounds a weapon can fire in a m inute (hereinafter
“rpm”) produces an index of energy delivered over
time which directly translates into the rapidity and
severity of the wounds it can produce.  We regard
this index as the best -available measure of
lethality.10 Our compilation appears in th e Table
published online at Kranefuss, Lee, “ MEpM” Recent
Post, https://lkranefuss.com/mepm/ (last accessed
Oct. 21, 2026), attached as appendix.11

10 Notably, it is not a statistical regression of how many crimes
are committed with a particular firearm or how many people
die as a result, or by suicide or accident which are imprecise
indicators of lethality.

11 In submitting our Table’s analysis of public information, we
observe that from time to time the Court may rely upon
guidance from an amicus to make even the most consequential
decisions of law. See, e.g., Teague v. Lane, 489 U.S. 288, 300
(1989) (“The question of retroactivity with regard to petitioner's
fair cross section claim has been raised only in an amicus
brief.”); Mapp v. Ohio, 367 U.S. 643, 646, n. 3 (1961) (applying
exclusionary rule to the States even although such a course of
action was urged only by amicus curiae).

12
 Using publicly-available data, the
semiautomatic handguns and even the heaviest bolt-
action rifles produce between 15,000 and 40,000 footpounds (ft. -lbs.) of energy  per minute. By contrast,
the AK -47 and paradigmatic semiautomatic rifles
(e.g., the AR- 15, Browning BAR, M1 Garand, and
Springfield M1A) (hereinafter “AR -15 rifle”) produce
60,000 to 108,000 foot-pounds per minute of MEpM.
 B. We submit that a principled distinction
may be drawn between firearms on either side of
this exponential leap in lethality. Thus, on one side,
semiautomatic handguns and all bolt -action rifles
are protected, see District of Columbia v. Heller , 554
U.S. 570 (2008). On the other, the various States are
left to regulate (or not) semiautomatic rifles within
their borders, with in equitable or analogical limits.
Any line -drawing in this area involves normative
choices. But, this one, we contend, is far more rooted
in objectivity than deciding whether a particular
“Arm” is “in common use” “for self-defense.”
 C. We explain what the Second Circuit got
right in Grant: that the right test at Step Two of the
NYSRPA v. Bruen , 597 U.S. 1 (2022) analysis is
whether a particular “Arm” is  “ unusually
dangerous,” and the right historical analogue is to
“bravado and affray” laws , Grant Pet. App. 30a -33a,
37a-49a, 67a-73a (Nathan, J., concurring) ; and what
Grant got wrong – failing to consider MEpM as the
basis to distinguish semiautomatic handguns and
AR-15 rifles.12 Bottom-line: MEpM provides a sound
basis for partially affirming the lower courts here,

12 We disagree with the Seventh Circuit that AR-15 rifles are
not “Arms” within the plain text of the Second Amendment.
Viramontes Pet. App. 2a-3a (citing Bevis v. City of Naperville,
85 F.4th 1175, 1185 (7th Cir. 2023).

13
and by implication, the First, Fourth, Ninth, and
D.C. Circuits 13 which have also u pheld overbroad
restrictions on both semiautomatic handguns and
AR-15 rifles.
 D. Finally, we find in t his Court’s
protection of the P eople’s privacy against new State
technologies which do not trespass on their “persons,
houses, papers, and effects,” U.S . Const. amend. IV,
an analogy for an “unusually dangerous” simpliciter
standard to regulate new MEpM- outlier firearms
without resort to any historical precursor-statute.
ARGUMENT
Chief Justice Roberts has observed that
“[w]hen confronting new concerns wrought by digital
technology, this Court has been careful not to
uncritically extend existing precedents.” Carpenter v.
United States , 585 U.S. 296, 318 (2018). Just last
term, in Chatrie v. United States, 146 S. Ct. 2193
(2026) the Court cleaved to first principles spacious
enough to constrain a geofence warrant that
gathered cell phone location data but d id not search
“persons, houses, papers, [or] effects.” U.S. Const.
amend. IV.

13  See Ocean State Tactical, LLC v. Rhode Island, 95 F.4th 38,
46 (1st Cir. 2024), cert. denied, 2025 U.S. LEXIS 2129 (2025);
Capen v. Campbell, 134 F.4th 660, 671 (1st Cir. 2025); Bianchi
v. Brown, 111 F.4th 438, 464-72 (4th Cir. 2024) (en banc), cert.
denied sub nom. Snope v. Brown, 145 S. Ct. 1534 (2025);
Duncan v. Bonta, 133 F.4th 852, 874 (9th Cir. 2025); Miller v.
Bonta, 2026 U.S. App. LEXIS 19416 (9th Cir. Jul. 1, 2026)
(submission vacated pending these cases); Hanson v. District of
Columbia, 120 F.4th 223, 237-38 (D.C. Cir. 2024), cert. denied,
2025 U.S. LEXIS 2221 (2025).

14
This case involves new concerns wr ought by a
new firearm technology. It calls upon the Court to
explicate what level of lethality in individual hands
is too much, or, if the test is empirical, whether that
decision should be left to legislatures. See Carpenter,
585 U.S. at 386 (Alito, J., dissenting) (legislation is
preferable “to respond to rapidly changing
technology”); id. at 390-394 (Gorsuch, J., dissenting)
(contours of “privacy” are better not “left to the
judicial imagination[,]” and if the test is empirical, it
should be left to leg islators). A majority of the Court
accepts that “the Fourth Amendment protects
people, not places,” Katz v. United States , 389 U.S.
347 (1967) (recognizing that electronic as well as
physical intrusions may violate the Fourth
Amendment). Likewise, t he Second Amendment
protects people, not guns , and at the periphery of
“unusually dangerous” firearms , is best left to
empirical test.
MEpM provides an empirical test of the AR-15
rifle’s lethality against other comparators, historical
and current. The results  lend themselves to a clear
bright line below which semiautomatic handguns
and bolt-action rifles are protected, and above which,
AR-15 rifles are not. As the Second Circuit found,
the historical test is best understood as whether a
firearm is “unusually dangerous” and the closest
statutory-precursor are “bravado and affray” laws.
Cinching that bright line is still subjective, but far
less so than “common use” or legislative- practice
doctrines. And, privileging “common use” which is
highly-regional, self-reported, or otherwise skewed to
“uncritically” calcify Second Amendment law
heightens our political division s. Conversely , if this
Court finds no Second Amendment right to “keep
and bear” an AR-15 rifle, the vast majority of current

15
owners will be ut terly unaffected as they live in the
40 States that choose not to regulate it.
On this basis, the Court should affirm that
legislatures may ban AR -15 rifles and remand the
cases for overbreadth analysis and procedural
protections.
A. History and Syntax Are “Consistent
with Common Sense” And Support the
“Unusually Dangerous” Test
Justice Barrett has observed that “[h]istory is
consistent with common sense: it demonstrates that
legislatures have the power to prohibit dangerous
people from possessing guns .” Rahimi, 602 U.S. at
(Barrett, J., concurring) (quoting Kanter v. Barr, 919
F.3d 437, 451, 464-465 (7th Cir. 2019) (Barrett, J.,
dissenting)). The lower court’s reading of history and
syntax in this case squares with common sense that
legislatures have the power to prohibit “unusually
dangerous” guns under an empirical standard. See
Grant Pet. App. 48a, 70a-73a.
History and Syntax.  The Second Cir cuit cited
Blackstone’s text and historical  linguistic evidence
that the Founders would have understood both
disjunctive and conjunctive phraseologies as a
grammatical hendiadys meaning one and the same
thing, i.e., “a ban on weapons that were ‘unusually
dangerous.’” Id. at 30a-33a & n.19; see also  id. at
70a-72a (Nathan, J., concurring) (“unusually
dangerous” is the doctrinal test most faithful to the
“variegated historical descriptions,” and even more,
the “historical reasons”) (emphasis in original). Thi s
seems persuasive on its own terms, but even more so
because it accords with common sense, and avoids a

16
case-dispositive test (“common use”) that sidesteps
dangerousness altogether.
The conjunctive test (“unusual and
dangerous”) urged by Petitioners and t he United
States as amicus, and favored by Justice Alito,
Caetano v. Massachusetts, 577 U.S. 411, 417 (2016)
(Alito, J., concurring), is neither textual nor deeply
historical, but pegged to a relatively -recent
“tradition” that started with regulation of saw n-off
shotguns under the National Firearms Act, 26
U.S.C. § 1132. United States v. Miller, 307 U.S. 174 ,
179 (1939); see Heller, 554 U.S. at  627 (“another
important limitation on the right to keep and carry
arms [was] fairly supported by the historical
tradition of prohibiting the carrying of ‘dangerous
and unusual weapons.’ See 4 Blackstone
[Commentaries on the Laws of England] 148 -149
(1769) [inter alia]”).14
Common sense. The conjunctive test’s most
severe failing is as an offense against common sense.
It makes the Second Amendment right turn on a
host of normative judgments about what number s of
individual owners 15 or of individual guns sold
constitute “common use.” Grant Pet. App. 30a, 32a.
After all, defining “unusual” i n terms of circulation

14 Miller used an interpretive method – asking “whether [the
weapon bore a] reasonable relationship to the preservation or
efficiency of a well regulated militia,” id.  at 178 -- that this
Court disavowed in Heller, 554 U.S. at 627.
15 Among the issues: how should so-called “super owners” who
own between eight and 140 weapons be counted (3% of the U.S.
adult population own nearly half of all civilian guns) -- by
person or by firearm?; and what significance, if any, should be
given to 15 U.S.C. § 7901 et seq., a liability shield for gun
manufacturers, that acts as a form of public subsidy for sales?

17
in society i s far more subjective than empirically
defining “dangerous.”  And, the value -choices only
compound if AR -15 owners’ motivations are also to
be quantified.
Petitioners assert that between 16 million and
26 million AR -15 rifles are in private hands
nationally. Pet. Brief at 11. Even if those self -
reported survey s are reliable, how is a court to
evaluate its threshold significance in a Nation of
270-million adults using “a body of evidence
susceptible of reasoned analysis”? McDonald  v. City
of Chicago , 561 U.S. 742, 804 (2010) (Scalia, J.,
concurring). And, if stun gun ownership by 200,000
civilians in 45  non-regulating states qualifies as
“common use,” see Caetano, 577 U.S. at 420 (Alito, J.,
concurring), one may rightly wonder are there any
teeth at all to “common use”?16
 Conversely, the “unusually dangerous”
MEpM test meets Justice Scalia’s insistence on an
empirical standard. See also  Caetano, 577 U.S. at
418 (Alito, J., concurring)  (“relative dangerousness”
must distinguish outliers among all “a rms” whose
very purpose is “to produce death or great bodily
harm”); see also Grant Pet. App. 32a (explaining the
logic of  applying “unusual” as a modifier and
“obvious fit” for “dangerous”).

16 The United States’ proposition that “[a] court should face no
trouble in concluding, for instance, that […] sword canes and
spears are not [in common use][.],” USA Amicus Brief, at 17,
suggests not.

18
B. The MEpM Points to an Empirical
Bright Line Test of “Unusual
Dangerousness”
Semiautomatic handguns.  Under Heller,
statistical evidence that a particular firearm has
been used or is favored by criminals is rightfully not
evidence of its dangerousness. Our MEpM Table
harmonizes with Heller , McDonald, and Bruen
because it shows a clear bright line, and
semiautomatic handguns fall on the protected side of
that line. In that sense, MEpM answers then- Judge
Kavanaugh’s search for any evidence of “a sensible
and principled constitutional line” between
semiautomatic handguns and rifles. Heller v. District
of Columbia , 670 F.3d 1244, 1269, 1286 n.14 (D.C.
Cir. 2011) (“ Heller II ”) (Kavanaugh, J., dissenting) ;
Snope v. Brown, 145 S. Ct. 1534 (2025) (Kavanaugh,
J., statement respecting the denial of certiorari) (“it
can be analyt ically difficult to distinguish the AR -
15[] [rifles] at issue here from the handguns at issue
in Heller. AR-15s are semi -automatic, but so too are
most handguns.”) It bears emphasizing that t he
MEpM coefficient of these firearms is  a principled
way to m easure lethality and thereby , to establish ,
by comparison with other protected firearms, an
empirical test for “unusual dangerousness”
simpliciter.
MEpM is a direct measure of energy per
minute, and energy is what damages any material or
body.  That is exactly what energy measures: a plate
dropped on the head of a pedestrian from a second
story window , a nd a concrete block from the tenth,
differ, precisely, in energy.  And ten concrete  blocks
per minute dropped on the same pedestrian inflicts
ten times the damage as one  per minute: this is

19
exactly what MepM measure s the equivalent of with
firearms. The metric is easy to understand and
captures the right things in exactly the ways things
should fit together – just as it would for concrete
blocks – precisely as an object ive measure should .
For this  reason,  Second Amendment protection of
AR-15 rifles simply does not “follow[] a fortiori from
Heller’s holding that it protects semiautomatic
handguns.” USA Amicus Brief, at 22.
The bright line test. Heller instructs that “the
enshrinement of constitutional rights necessarily
takes certain policy choices off the table.” Heller, 554
U.S. at 636. But, deference to legislative empiricism
that “x” amount of MEpM invests too much
firepower in private hands is not an untethered
“policy choice.” The 50% increase in MEpM from the
most powerful bolt -action rifle (the Winchester M70
African) to the AK-47 rifle (the least-powerful AR-15
style rifle), presents an obvious categorical line.
This is neither interest balancing, cost-benefit
analysis, nor a new and different flavor of strict or
intermediate scrutiny. Instead, it flows from the
principle of Heller that the core Second Amendment
right to keep and bear arms is not unlimited , Heller,
554 U.S. at 626, and one plain  limit is objective
“unusual dangerousness.” The legislature, rather
than the judiciary, is the proper branch to draw that
line where empirical MEpM lethality greatly exceeds
those of semi automatic handguns and bolt -action
rifles protected by the contours of the right.
Caetano v. Massachusetts, 577 U.S. 411 (per
curiam) is consistent with this approach because
MEpM does not concern itself with any non-relevant
characteristics of the firearm, e.g. , its post -
enactment pedigree, usefulness in warfare or in

20
crime. According to our Table, the AR- 15 rifle is  a
modern outlier firearm in terms of its exponentially
outsized firepower . That simply means the various
States may choose to regulate it in ways that will not
pass muster for semiautomatic handguns or bolt -
action rifles. The proper judicial inquiry, in our view,
focuses on whether the legislature has applied
neutral, common-sense criteria for assessing modern
outlier weapons, not whether the States themselves
are “outliers.”17 We suggest to the Court that MEpM,
a measure implicitly adopted by the lower court, is
the way to go  in considering whether certain
presumptively-covered “arms” are, by virtue of their
extreme lethality, unprotected  from specific and
appropriate state Legislative action.18
C. “Bravado and Affray” Laws Provide a
Historical Analogy from Yesteryear’s
Group Violence to Today’s Armed
Madman
Going armed laws, also known as “bravado
and affray” laws, “prohibited riding or going armed,
with dangerous or unusual weapons, to terrify the
good people of the land.” Rahimi , 602 U.S. at 697

17 Amicus Professor Amar would have the Court find dispositive
that 40-States encompassing two-thirds of America’s
population permit civilian ownership of AR-15’s, but he
suggests the Court “avoid premature judicial ‘lock-in’” that nips
reform movements in the bud when it comes to the 13-States
(all of them electorally “Blue”) that ban large capacity
magazines (“LCM’s”). Amar Amicus Brief, at 35-36. The
obvious riposte is what makes 13, not 10, the magic number for
judicial hands-off, and where’s the objectivity in that?

18 Other novel weapons, e.g., hunter-killer drones, may require
other empirical tests for assessing dangerousness in due
course.

21
(cleaned up); see also Bruen , 597 U.S. at 46 (quoting
4 Willia m Blackstone, Commentaries *148 -49
(defining the offense of affray to include going armed
with “dangerous or unusual” weapons); Grant Pet.
App. 31a n.18 (same).
Grant found a relevant historical tradition of
restricting unusually dangerous weapons when
legislatures observed these weapons’ “unprecedented
lethality” in “use in terror or to perpetrate mass
casualties.” Id. at 59a-60a & n.40 . It canvassed the
history of laws restricting, inter alia, launcegays,
Bowie knives, dirks, Thompson submachine guns,
and sawn-off shotguns, id. at 51a-58a, before
focusing on the capacity of semiautomatic rifles with
“vastly increased” “capacity and [] rapidity of firing.”
Id. at 38a ( quoting Hanson v. District of Columbia,
120 F.4th 223, 240 (D.C. Cir. 2024), cert. denied ,
2025 U.S. LEXIS 2221 (2025) ) (cleaned up). But, the
Second Circuit did not muster the best evidence to
quantify the effect of this new technology in
dramatically enhancing MEpM as an objective
measure of its lethality vis-à-vis relevant comparator
handguns and rifles. See Kranefuss, Lee, “ MEpM”
Recent Post, https://lkranefuss.com/mepm/ (last
accessed Oct. 21, 2026), attached as appendix.
Our MEpM Table quantifies just how
dramatically the technological advancement of the
AR-15 enhances firepower. In our view, “affray” laws
are the right historical analogue , albeit at an
understandably high -level of generality, for the
reason given by the Second Circuit: “The Founders
faced no problem comparable to a single gunman
carrying out a mass murder in seconds.” Grant Pet.
App. at 43a. The Table makes this point clearly: A

22
single person wielding an AR -15 rifle has all the
MEpM, or more, of a historical posse.
The Second Circuit found its analogue in the
Founder’s era 1770 Boston Massacre, noting that
“seven British soldiers firing flintlock muskets into a
crowd managed to take only five lives. ” Grant Pet.
App. 41a. While that comparison lacks the precision
of our Table, the point remains the same: the AR -15
rifle vests an exponentially -higher amount of
firepower in i ndividual hands beyond any other
historical or current firearm. To borrow from popular
culture, i t would take eight  Inspector Callahans,
each emptying their 6 -shot . 44 Magnum revolvers
(“the most powerful handgun in the world”) three
times in a minute to equal the firepower of one
person armed with an M1 Garand rifle, a mid- range
AR-15 archetype, that expends 85,219 ft -pounds per
minute of MEpM, firing 30 -rounds in that same
timeframe. See, e.g. , Dirty Harry , Internet Movie
Firearms Database, https://www.imfdb.org/wiki/
Dirty_Harry (last visited Oct. 5, 2026).
That, in a nutshell, is why t he Second
Amendment’s text and historical tradition do not bar
legislatures of the various States from regulating
possession or distribution of such an outlie r firearm
within their borders.  Professor Amar is persuasive
that the “hunt for [ Founding-era regulatory]
precursors” (even if not insistent on “dead ringers”)
is inapposite when confronting a dramatic
technological change that creates out -sized
individual power.19 Amar Amicus Brief at 32-33. We

19  We agree with Professor Amar that the Founders and
Reconstructionists simply did not have to contend with, and
therefore had no cause to regulate, the possibility that a single

23
also agree that sensitivity to our “deeply -polarized”20
Nation counsels for an approach that permits
minority (Blue) State regulation of objectively-outlier
firearms. This allows individual States to evaluate
those interests differently at the periphery of the
Second Amendment right against those collective
rights elsewhere enshrined to “ensure domestic
tranquility” and “promote general welfare”
(Preamble), or reserved to the States (Tenth
Amendment). See, e.g.,  The Fe deralist No. 84
(Alexander Hamilton); Dobbs v. Jackson Women's
Health Org. , 597 U.S. 215, 302 (2022) (noting that
prior decisions “enflamed debate and deepened
divisions,” and returning authority to regulate
abortion to the people and their elected
representatives). There, as here, “the people of the
various States may evaluate those interests
differently[,]” id. at 256, especially along partisan
lines, and this Court should not enflame divisions by
removing it from the People’s elected
representatives.
D. Fourth Amendment Jurisprudence
Offers a Pragmatic Approach for
Constraining New Technologies
In Bruen, 597 U.S. at 27, this Court
acknowledged that “cases implicating unprecedented
societal concerns or dramatic technological changes
may require a more nua nced approach.” Thus, while
“the meaning of the constitutional text is fixed at the
time of its ratification and [] the ‘discoverable
historical meaning … is authoritative in most

madman could “kill dozens in seconds,” id. at 33, which is a
design feature of the AR-15 rifle’s singular MEpM.

20 Amar Amicus Brief at 37.

24
circumstances,’” Rahimi, 602 U.S. at 737 (Barrett, J.,
concurring), this, to o, is not without limits. The
Fourth Amendment case law shows one possible
parallel between privacy and dangerousness here.
The phrase “dramatic technological change”
itself first appears in this Court’s modern Fourth
Amendment jurisprudence as it began to adapt to a
world where common -law trespass has become
increasingly unnecessary to many forms of
surveillance. See, e.g. , United States v. Jones, 565
U.S. 400, 429 -30 (2012) (Alito, J., concurring) (“In
circumstances involving dramatic technological
change, the best solution to privacy concerns may be
legislative.… to gauge changing public attitudes, to
draw detailed lines, and to balance privacy and
public safety in a comprehensive way.”); cf. United
States v. Knotts , 460 U.S. 276, 283 (1983)
(Rehnquist, J .) (“if such dragnet -type law
enforcement practices as respondent envisions
[twenty-four hour surveillance of any citizen] should
eventually occur, there will be time enough then to
determine whether different constitutional
principles may be applicable.”).
Thirty-five years later, when police used
wireless cell -phone site location data  cataloging a
suspect’s movements in toto to confirm his proximity
to the sites of four robberies, the Court (Roberts,
C.J.) held that such a search implicated F ourth
Amendment privacy interests and required a
warrant. Carpenter v. United States, 585 U.S. 296. In
that way, Carpenter  fulfilled Knotts’ openness to
“expand [its] conception of the [Fourth] Amendment”
to protect individual rights in the face of (1)
“innovations in surveillance tools,” “advancing
technology,” “a new phenomenon,” “an entirely new

25
species of business record,” and (2) the ubiquity of
cell phones as “almost a ‘feature of human anatomy’”
to achieve “near perfect surveillance.” Id. at 304,
309, 311 -12, 318 (citation omitted). This case asks
the Court to expand its conception of the Second
Amendment in similarly reckoning with the “seismic
shift in [] technology,” id. at 313, that makes the AR-
15 rifle so much more dangerous than any of its
comparators.
In United States v. Jones, 565 U.S. at 408-09,
411, the Court (Scalia, J.) clarified that “ Katz [ v.
United States, 389 U.S. 347 (1967)] did not narrow
the Fourth Amendment’s scope[,]” but added the
privacy-test to the trespassory test, calling it a
necessary “novelty” to apply “at a minimum the
degree of protection [the 19th century right ] afforded
when it was adopted.” 21 Just last Term, this Court
applied the doctrine to hold that police use of a
“geofence warrant” to identify a robber by his cell -
phone’s proximity to a bank when the crime occurred
also constituted a search under the Fourth
Amendment. Chatrie v. United States, 146 S. Ct.
2193.

21 While Justice Scalia once derided Justice Harlan’s
“expectation of privacy” as a “fuzzy standard,” Minnesota v.
Carter, 525 U.S. 83, 91 (1998) (Scalia, J., concurring), by the
time Jones was decided, he, like the majority thereafter in
Carpenter and Chatrie, recognized its relevance to the
“reasonableness” of a search or seizure employing new
investigatory technologies. At the same time, Justice Scalia
confirmed his underlying view that where the answer “is not
remotely contained in the Constitution, … it is left -- as many,
indeed most, important questions are left -- to the judgment of
state and federal legislators.” Id. at 98. It would be odd if the
institutional-modesty tenet of originalism applied everywhere –
except the Second Amendment.

26
In all of these c ases, th is Court has hewn to
first principles: the basic purpose” of the Fourth
Amendment” “is to safeguard the privacy and
security of individuals against arbitrary invasions by
governmental officials.” Id.  at 2204- 05. Time and
again, the Court has rejected a “mechanical
interpretation” that fixates solely on the historical -
trespassory form of  infringement. Id. at 2205- 06 &
n.7 (collecting cases) , 2213 (discussing the cell -
phone’s pervasive role in dragnet -like new
surveillance technologies that mine it for sensitive
personal information ). Bottom line: b ecause “the
Founders could not have imagined such a
technology,” resort to their understanding that
Americans have “the right to be let alone” is
necessary to interpret the Amendment in
contemporary society. Id. at 2216-17.
The parallel here: like reasonable expectations
of privacy, an empirical doctrine of “unusual
dangerousness” simpliciter may be useful in
evaluating whether the AR -15 rifle lie s beyond the
scope of the Second Amendment right because of its
dramatic technological advancement in lethality .
Such a  doctrine subjects to the constraints of
empiricism the power of legislature s as the
democratic will of the people to regulate (or not) the
people’s right to keep and bear unduly -powerful
arms.
E. This Court Should Remand the Cases
for Overbreadth and Specific
Applications
Assuming this Court accepts MEpM as an
empirical measure of the AR -15 rifle’s lethality
which puts it outside the people’s right to keep and
bear arms  and answers the certiorari question , the

27
lower courts in these cases have much work to do.
First, the statutes may be facially overbroad in
banning many  models of semiautomatic handguns
with lower MEpM’s . Second, the lower courts must
answer whether AR-15-style firearms not designed
to be fired from the shoulder are more properly
classified as protected handguns  by reference to
their MEpM’s. See, e.g. , Grant Pet. App. 13a -14a &
n.10 (summarizing Conn. Gen. Stat. § 53 -
202a(1)(G)). Third, if “bravado and affray” laws
provide the precursor-a nalogue predicate rather
than adopting “unusually dangerous” simpliciter, the
lower courts must determine whether the laws are
also overbroad in banning t he “keeping” of AR-15
rifles in the home rather than “bearing” them
outside of it. Fourth, do fair notice and reliance
interests bar the application of Code of Ordinances of
Cook County § 54-212 to current owners of any AR-
15 rifles, which criminalizes possession without the
grandfathering of Conn. Gen. Stat. § 53-202a(7).

28
CONCLUSION
This Court should hold that the Second and
Fourteenth Amendments do not  guarantee the right
to possess AR -15 platform and similar
semiautomatic rifles, and remand the cases for
further proceedings.
